title: [HashiCorp] Banking at machine speed: Securing access across cloud, AI, and hybrid environments
summary: Banks have long invested in identity and access management to protect critical systems, customer data, and financial transactions. But cloud adoption, automation, and AI are changing who and what requires access.Applications, workloads, services and AI-enabled systems all need access to banking resources. As these environments become more distributed and automated, security leaders must maintain control without adding persistent credentials, fragmented policies, or governance gaps.What security teams are facing today goes beyond managing a growing number of identities. They must determine what autonomous systems can access, which actions they can perform, and how those activities are monitored as operations move at machine speed.How can financial institutions manage access across cloud, AI, and hybrid environments while supporting compliance, auditability, and operational resilience?Identity is becoming a governance challengeModern banking depends on automation. Applications interact with databases and cloud services. Infrastructure is provisioned dynamically. Fraud detection platforms analyze transactions in real time. AI-enabled systems may need access to transaction platforms, fraud detection services, customer data sources, and operational workflows, creating new access-control and governance considerations.A recurring theme during the recent AI Governance for Banking: Securing Agentic AI at Scale roundtable was the need for clearer controls around AI decision-making. As AI agents gain access to more systems and data, the focus shifts to defining what they should be authorized to do. That requires policies, accountability, and oversight that support regulatory compliance and AI risk management. Each workload, application, and service requires access to resources, and every request must be authenticated, authorized, and governed. As machine identities spread across public cloud, private cloud, and on-premises infrastructure, security teams need controls that can work consistently across environments. The real concern is how credentials are created, distributed, and used at machine speed, often across systems that span multiple teams, tools, and environments. Where credential risk accumulatesApplications rely on secrets, tokens, certificates, and credentials to connect with databases, APIs, and infrastructure services. Over time, these credentials can become dispersed across tools and environments, creating long-lived access, fragmented controls, and visibility gaps.Security teams need to know where credentials reside, what’s using them, and whether the access is still required. They must also provide evidence that access to critical systems is controlled, monitored, and auditable. Agents may interact with multiple systems, APIs, and data sources to complete a task. Without strong identity controls, organizations can struggle to understand what authority has been delegated, how access is being used, and whether activity remains aligned to policy.For organizations investing in banking automation, access governance now extends beyond employees and contractors. Machine identity, nonhuman identity security, secrets management, and credential management are becoming core requirements for securing AI agents, APIs, and automated workflows. As AI adoption grows in banking, reducing credential sprawl and strengthening API security are becoming important elements of a broader AI governance framework. Govern access across hybrid environmentsFor security leaders, machine identity management is both a security responsibility and governance requirement. Access policies must work across cloud and on-premises environments, even as workloads change and infrastructure scales.A centralized, policy-based approach gives teams a consistent way to authenticate machine identities, issue time-limited credentials, apply least-privilege policies, and preserve an auditable record of access activity across environments.Banks preparing for wider AI adoption will need these controls in place long before large-scale autonomous operations become commonplace.Roundtable participants emphasized that AI initiatives require the same level of oversight, policy enforcement, and accountability already expected of other critical banking systems. That visibility must extend from identity assignment and model interactions through API access and execution. Those capabilities support AI compliance, cloud governance, and operational resilience while improving visibility into autonomous activity. The case for identity-based securityIdentity-based security changes how access is granted. Instead of using a static credential stored in an application or configuration file, a workload authenticates with a verified identity. Policy determines what it can access, and a credential can be issued for a specific purpose and a limited period. This model can help financial institutions:Reduce credential and access riskApply least-privilege access more consistentlyLimit reliance on persistent credentialsMaintain a clearer, auditable record of access activityImprove machine identity and service account managementProtect the credentials behind open banking and partner APIsSupport regulatory compliance and operational resilience objectivesConsistent controls can reduce credential-management overhead and simplify governance of sensitive access across cloud, on-premises, and hybrid environments.Solutions like Vault enable this model by authenticating machine identities and issuing dynamic, policy-based credentials rather than relying on static secrets.Prepare for agentic AIAgentic AI brings added urgency to an issue banks already face. As autonomous systems take on more operational tasks, access decisions increasingly occur without direct human involvement. Governing that activity requires organizations to verify identity, limit authority, enforce policy, and maintain auditable records of access at runtime.During the AI Governance for Banking discussion, speakers noted that successful AI adoption depends on more than model performance. Organizations need operational discipline, visibility across workflows, enforceable controls, and clear ownership of outcomes. These capabilities are critical as banks address AI risk management objectives, Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) compliance initiatives, and hybrid cloud security requirements.Vault, together with the IBM® Agent Identity capability, gives banks the foundation to run AI agents safely across hybrid cloud environments. Agent Identity registers each agent and ties its delegated authority to a human user. Vault turns that delegated authority into identity-based access, issuing dynamic, short-lived secrets scoped to least privilege and capturing every request in a complete audit trail. Every action traces back to an accountable person, and access can be revoked at the source the moment something looks wrong.The solution supports the outcomes security leaders are accountable for: stronger governance, improved auditability, reduced operational burden, and greater confidence in access controls as banking infrastructure becomes more automated.Learn more about VaultBanking infrastructure is becoming increasingly automated, prompting many institutions to reassess how machine identities, secrets, and access policies are governed.Many organizations are also evaluating how AI governance, AI compliance, cloud governance, and resilience requirements fit within wider security and risk-management strategies.Explore how financial institutions are approaching risk remediation, open banking API security, nonhuman identity governance, and secure AI adoption with financial services risk remediation.Explore risk remediation strategiesRelated ContentFrom zero trust to continuous trust: Securing autonomous AI systems4/21/2026 | HashiCorp

title: [Kubernetes] Kubernetes v1.37: Tracking When a PersistentVolumeClaim Was Last Used (Beta)
summary: Kubernetes v1.37 promotes the PersistentVolumeClaimUnusedSinceTime feature gate to Beta (enabled by default). With this feature, the PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) protection controller adds an Unused condition to each PVC, telling you whether any running pod currently references it — no custom tooling or cross-referencing required. For the API definition of PVC conditions, see the PersistentVolumeClaim API reference. Read on to learn how the Unused condition works and how to use it. Why track PVC usage?In large-scale Kubernetes clusters, it is common for users to create PVCs and then delete the associated pods without cleaning up the storage, because Kubernetes does not automatically delete PVCs when their pods are removed (to protect against accidental data loss). Over time, these orphaned PVCs may accumulate, silently consuming storage capacity and driving up cloud costs. Before Kubernetes v1.37, it was easy to identify an unused PersistentVolume, but much harder to determine whether a PVC was still being used. Doing so required cross-referencing pods, PersistentVolumes, and PVCs over a potentially large window of time. Administrators often resorted to custom monitoring pipelines or scripts to answer a seemingly simple question: "Is anything actually using this volume?" The PersistentVolumeClaimUnusedSinceTime feature solves this by making the answer available natively in the PVC status. Once the feature is enabled, every PVC gets an Unused condition managed by the PVC protection controller. User stories Storage administrator: "I want to know which PVCs in my cluster are not being used by any pod so I can safely identify orphaned volumes and schedule them for deletion." DevOps engineer: "I want to list PVCs that have the Unused condition set to True so I can automate cleanup in development environments." How does it work?The PVC protection controller — which already watches pods to enforce the storage object in use protection — now also manages a new Unused condition on PVCs. The condition works as follows: Scenario Condition status Reason No non-terminal pods reference the PVC Unused=True NoPodsUsingPVC At least one running or pending pod references the PVC Unused=False PodUsingPVC A few details worth noting: Terminated pods don't count: A pod that has completed (phase Succeeded or Failed) does not keep the PVC marked as in use. This means batch jobs with restartPolicy: Never won't prevent the PVC from becoming Unused=True after they finish. Pending pods do count: Even an unschedulable pod (for example, one with an impossible node selector) still counts as using the PVC. The intent to use the volume is enough. Multiple pods: If several pods reference the same PVC, the condition transitions to Unused=True only after the *last" non-terminated pod is removed or terminates. Using lastTransitionTime to find when a PVC became idleLike every Kubernetes condition, the Unused condition carries a standard lastTransitionTime field. This means you get a useful bonus for free: when the condition transitions from False to True, the lastTransitionTime records exactly when the PVC became idle. You can use this timestamp to answer questions like "how long has this PVC been sitting unused?" — for example, to find PVCs that have been idle for more than 30 days (see the example query below). What changed from Alpha to Beta?Kubernetes v1.36 introduced this feature as Alpha, where you had to enable the PersistentVolumeClaimUnusedSinceTime feature gate explicitly. For Beta in v1.37, the feature gate is enabled by default, and the feature has full end-to-end test coverage. How to use itSince the feature is Beta and enabled by default in Kubernetes v1.37, the Unused condition will appear on PVCs automatically. Here is a walkthrough to see it in action: Create a PVC: apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata: name: my-data spec: accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce resources: requests: storage: 1Gi After a short time, inspect the PVC conditions: kubectl get pvc my-data -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}' | jq . You should see an Unused condition with status True and reason NoPodsUsingPVC: { "lastProbeTime": null, "lastTransitionTime": "2026-09-14T12:03:11Z", "message": "No pods are currently referencing this PVC", "reason": "NoPodsUsingPVC", "status": "True", "type": "Unused" } Create a pod that uses the PVC: apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: my-app spec: containers: - name: app image: busybox command:  volumeMounts: - name: data mountPath: /data volumes: - name: data persistentVolumeClaim: claimName: my-data Check the condition again — it should now show Unused=False: kubectl get pvc my-data -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions.status}' Output: False Delete the pod and wait for the condition to transition back to Unused=True: kubectl delete pod my-app kubectl get pvc my-data -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}' The condition should show Unused=True with reason NoPodsUsingPVC again. Finding unused PVCs across the clusterTo list all PVCs that have been unused for more than 30 days, you can use a command like: Note:This command uses jq, a command-line JSON processor. kubectl get pvc -A -o json | jq -r ' .items | select(.status.conditions? | select(.type=="Unused" and .status=="True")) | select( (.status.conditions | select(.type=="Unused") | .lastTransitionTime) as $t | (now - ($t | fromdateiso8601)) > (30 * 86400) ) | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name) unused since \(.status.conditions | select(.type=="Unused") | .lastTransitionTime)" ' What's next?Depending on feedback and adoption, the Kubernetes project intends to graduate this feature to General Availability (GA) in a future release. If you have feedback on this feature, please open an issue in the kubernetes/kubernetes repository. To learn more about this enhancement, refer to KEP-5541: PersistentVolumeClaim last used time. Getting involvedThe Kubernetes project always welcomes new contributors. If you would like to get involved, you can join us at SIG Storage. If you would like to share feedback, you can do so on our public Slack channel (visit https://slack.k8s.io/ for an invitation if you need one). title: [Slack Engineering] From SSH to REST: A Security-Driven Modernization of Slack’s EMR Data Pipelines
summary: Excerpt By 2024, Slack’s data platform had accumulated 700+ SSH-based operators orchestrating critical data pipelines. We’re talking daily search indexing that processed terabytes of data, analytics jobs powering business intelligence, the whole shebang. Every single one of these jobs required direct SSH access to production AWS Elastic MapReduce (EMR) clusters. We had a massive security surface, and we couldn’t move forward on any infrastructure modernization. Not ideal. We needed to eliminate SSH entirely. The solution? Migrate all 700+ jobs to a REST-based architecture. This is the story of how we killed SSH entirely, across 8 data regions, with zero downtime. How We Got Here Slack’s data platform was built around 2017 with a straightforward pattern. Airflow, our data pipeline orchestrator, needed to run jobs on EMR clusters, and SSH was the most direct path. Connect to the EMR master node, execute a command, done. Simple. # The old way - simple, but problematic task = SSHOperator( task_id='run_spark_job', ssh_conn_id='emr_master', command='spark-submit /path/to/job.py', ) This pattern proliferated across the platform. Teams built custom SSH-based operators for different use cases (because hey, if SSH works for Spark, why not everything else). By the time we took stock, we had 700+ jobs in production running everything from MapReduce jobs to AWS CLI commands to custom Python scripts. It worked. But it came with some potential problems. The Real Cost of SSH Potential security risks included: Direct SSH access to compute clusters increases the potential attack surface Key distribution and rotation across orchestration workers adds operational overhead Achieving fine-grained audit granularity typically requires correlating logs across multiple systems Permission management can grow complex, often requiring dedicated security groups and custom configurations Operations were painful: Jobs ran directly on EMR master nodes instead of being distributed, causing resource contention When Kubernetes pods restarted, SSH connections broke and jobs failed Long-running jobs became “zombies” that kept executing after their connections terminated No reliable way to determine if a job succeeded or failed when connections dropped (not ideal when you’re processing terabytes) We were blocked: Couldn’t start the path for Spark on Kubernetes nor EMR on AWS Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) (required eliminating SSH dependencies first) Couldn’t complete our Whitecastle initiative because we needed to move the last main-account EMR clusters to child accounts Whitecastle is Slack’s initiative to migrate AWS infrastructure to child accounts for improved security and network isolation. Building the Next Evolution of Cloud Networks at Slack: A Retrospective Couldn’t implement proper job monitoring and observability An example problem: The Search Infrastructure team’s pipeline builds Solr search indexes from terabytes of data daily. This pipeline powers Slack’s search functionality. Any disruption affects search quality for millions of users. And it was relying on SSH-based job submission with all the reliability problems mentioned above. Not great. Understanding the Foundation: REST-Based Job Submission Before diving into the solution, let’s establish what REST-based job submission actually means (and why it matters). The Problem with SSH When you SSH into a machine and run a command, you’re creating a direct, stateful connection. If that connection drops (say your Kubernetes pod restarts), the command might keep running, might fail, or might leave orphaned processes hanging around. You’ve got no reliable way to reconnect and check status. It’s like hanging up mid-phone call and hoping the other person finishes the conversation. The REST Alternative Modern compute engines (YARN, Trino, Snowflake) expose HTTP APIs for job submission. Instead of maintaining a connection, you: POST a job request → receive a job ID GET job status using the ID → check if it’s running, completed, or failed DELETE the job → cleanly cancel, if needed The job lifecycle is managed server-side. Your client can crash and restart, and the job keeps running while you can still query its status. Much better. The YARN Piece For Hadoop workloads (MapReduce, Spark, Hive), YARN is the resource manager with a REST API for job submission. But here’s the catch: YARN’s API is designed for Hadoop jobs. What about the 300+ CLI-based jobs running arbitrary shell commands like aws s3 sync or hadoop distcp? That’s where YARN Distributed Shell comes in. This was the key breakthrough that made this whole migration possible. The Breakthrough: YARN Distributed Shell Migrating Spark and Hive jobs was more straightforward. Spark has the Livy REST API and Hive has HiveServer2. But MapReduce jobs and the 300+ CLI-based jobs running arbitrary shell commands? Those were the hard parts. They didn’t have ready-made REST APIs. We brainstormed multiple approaches. Our requirements were clear: Simple REST-based solution: fits naturally into our architecture Existing authentication and authorization mechanisms: no custom security layer to build and maintain Open-source protocols: leverage standard YARN APIs, not proprietary solutions Minimal complexity: no building and maintaining custom job execution infrastructure Some ideas we considered: Building a custom wrapper service to execute commands remotely Using remote execution frameworks like Ansible or Salt Creating a new job type in YARN from scratch All of these felt too complex, required custom security implementations, or introduced new dependencies we’d have to maintain. Not great options. Then we discovered YARN’s Distributed Shell. It’s a little-known feature (org.apache.hadoop.yarn.applications.distributedshell.ApplicationMaster) that allows any shell script to run in a proper YARN container with resource allocation and lifecycle management. And here’s the kicker: it was already part of YARN, used the same REST APIs, and required no custom security layer. It was perfect. Here’s how it works: 1. Upload your command to S3 For example, we could upload the following script (command.sh) to s3://bucket/ # command.sh aws s3 sync /tmp/data/ s3://bucket/output/ 2. Submit to YARN with Distributed Shell configuration { "application-type": "MAPREDUCE", "am-container-spec": { "commands": { "command": "{{JAVA_HOME}}/bin/java org.apache.hadoop.yarn.applications.distributedshell.ApplicationMaster ..." }, "environment": { "DISTRIBUTEDSHELLSCRIPTLOCATION": "s3://bucket/command.sh", "DISTRIBUTEDSHELLSCRIPTLEN": "548", "DISTRIBUTEDSHELLSCRIPTTIMESTAMP": "1768529627000" } } } 3. YARN allocates a container, downloads the script, and executes it: Yarn manages: Proper resource limits (memory, vCores) Container isolation Retry and fault tolerance Clean cancellation Proper logging through YARN UI This architectural decision unlocked the migration of all SSH-based jobs. Not just Hadoop workloads, but any shell command. Whether it was aws s3 sync, hadoop distcp, or custom Python scripts, they could all run in proper YARN containers. Game changer. Figure 1: YARN Distributed Shell job submission flow showing how arbitrary shell commands are executed in YARN containers through Quarry. The Solution: Quarry Now that we understand the advantages of REST-based job submission and how we can migrate each existing job type, we’re just missing one thing: an orchestrator. Enter Quarry, Slack’s REST-based job submission gateway. Quarry was originally built to provide a unified interface for submitting jobs across multiple compute engines (EMR/YARN, Trino, Snowflake). It already solved authentication, reliability, and observability challenges. For SSH deprecation, it turned out to be exactly what we needed. What Quarry Does Quarry sits between various services and compute engines (Airflow being the biggest user), handling: Authentication: Service-to-service tokens instead of SSH keys Job submission: REST APIs to YARN, Trino, and Snowflake State tracking: Server-side monitoring of job status Lifecycle management: Clean cancellation and cleanup through REST APIs Observability: Structured logs, metrics, and tracing for all job submissions The Architecture Shift Before: Airflow → SSH Connection → EMR Master Node → Execute Command After: Airflow → Quarry REST API → YARN ResourceManager → EMR Container Instead of establishing SSH connections, Airflow operators make HTTP requests to Quarry. Quarry submits jobs to YARN and polls for status. If an Airflow pod restarts, the job keeps running, and Quarry maintains the connection. Figure 2: Architecture comparison showing the shift from SSH-based direct execution to REST-based job submission through Quarry and YARN. The Quarry Advantage With YARN Distributed Shell support, Quarry became our universal job submission gateway. Whether you’re running a Spark job, a Hive query, or a simple shell script, it all goes through the same REST API. No SSH credentials. No direct cluster access. Just REST API calls with proper authentication and server-side job tracking. The Migration Journey We knew from the start this wasn’t going to be a quick fix. We had 700+ production jobs across 8 independent data regions, each with unique network configurations and data sovereignty requirements. Critical workloads, like search indexing, couldn’t tolerate any downtime. So yeah, we needed a plan. The Approach: Incremental and Phased Phase 1 – Proof of Concept: Started with pilot jobs to validate the Quarry-based approach. Built the first Quarry operators and tested in dev environments. Phase 2 – Security Review: Engaged security teams to plan credential elimination and ensure the REST-based approach met security requirements. Phase 3 – OKR-Driven Execution: Made it a Key Result with executive visibility. This created accountability and kept it prioritized. We hit the 80% migration milestone during this phase. Phase 4 – Bulk Migration: Heavy cross-team coordination to migrate remaining workloads across all regions. Multiple teams (Search Infrastructure, Data Engineering & Analytics, ML Services) worked in parallel. Phase 5 – Final Cleanup: Completed overlooked DAGs and deprecated all legacy SSH-based operators. Achieved 100% completion. Migration by the Numbers 700+ jobs migrated across 7 operator types 8 independent data regions with coordinated rollouts 5 teams transitioned to new operators Zero downtime for business-critical services Completed in 3 quarters, from initial pilot to 100% SSH elimination The Challenges We Hit No migration this size goes smoothly. Here are the biggest obstacles we ran into (and how we dealt with them). Challenge 1: Virtual Memory Check Failures During migration of a data export DAG, we hit unexpected failures. Jobs that’d been running fine via SSH were now failing with vmem (virtual memory) check errors. What gives? The root cause: SSH commands ran directly on the master node, bypassing YARN’s resource enforcement entirely. Quarry submits jobs properly to YARN, which actually enforces resource limits. The vmem check was rejecting containers that exceeded virtual memory limits (which SSH had been quietly ignoring). The fix: Following AWS best practices, we disabled vmem checks across all clusters: "yarn.nodemanager.vmem-check-enabled": "false" AWS explicitly recommends this because virtual memory accounting in Linux can be unreliable, and physical memory limits are sufficient. (Also, it’s worth noting that vmem checks have been a source of spurious failures for years in the Hadoop ecosystem.) Lesson learned: When migrating from SSH to proper YARN submission, expect to encounter resource limit issues that were previously invisible. SSH hides a lot of problems. Test thoroughly in dev environments before production rollout. Challenge 2: Network Segregation and EKM Connectivity During migration of dev search infrastructure jobs from one dev cluster to a staging analytics cluster, a task failed with an EKM (Enterprise Key Management) connectivity timeout. Great. Error: com.amazon.ws.emr.hadoop.fs.shaded.com.amazonaws.SdkClientException: Unable to execute HTTP request: Connect to sts.amazonaws.com:443 failed: connect timed out The root cause: the original cluster had network routing configured to reach the necessary key management endpoints. The staging analytics cluster, operating in a stricter network segment, did not have equivalent connectivity and correctly so. The failure surfaced a hidden dependency on network topology that wasn’t captured in the job’s configuration. The fix: We moved search infrastructure tasks to a dev ETL cluster with proper routing to dev services. For tasks requiring production Hive catalogs, we kept them in staging. We also scaled up the dev ETL cluster to handle the additional workload. Lesson learned: Network topology matters. Like, really matters. Understand network segregation and account boundaries before deciding which cluster runs which jobs. Dev jobs need dev network access, prod jobs need prod network access. The migration revealed hidden dependencies that SSH had been quietly papering over. Challenge 3: Multi-Region Complexity Slack operates EMR clusters across 8 independent data regions to support data sovereignty requirements. This meant the SSH deprecation wasn’t a single migration. It was effectively 8 parallel migrations, each with its own special set of challenges. Fun times. The Complexity Configuration management: Each region required separate Quarry configurations, cluster endpoints, and network routing rules Testing overhead: Every code change needed validation across all 8 regions before production rollout (multiply your testing time by 8) Staggered deployments: Couldn’t deploy to all regions simultaneously. Had to roll out region by region. Region-specific issues: Network configurations, data sovereignty rules, and cluster versions varied by region Our Approach Validated changes in a single pilot region (typically US-based for faster iteration) Documented region-specific configuration requirements Built region-aware Quarry operators that could handle regional differences Rolled out to remaining regions incrementally, learning from each deployment Maintained separate tracking for each region’s migration progress Lesson learned: Multi-region infrastructure significantly multiplies migration complexity. The effort isn’t just N times harder. It’s N times harder with unique failure modes for each region. Budget extra time for cross-region coordination and region-specific debugging. (Seriously, budget more time than you think.) The Results We achieved 100% SSH elimination. Every production job now runs through Quarry with REST-based submission. Here’s what we gained. Security Wins Eliminated SSH access to all production EMR clusters across 8 independent data regions, which massively reduced our attack surface. We replaced SSH key distribution with service-to-service token authentication, and gained proper audit trails through REST API logging. Every job submission now has structured logs through Quarry. No more “who ran that command?” mysteries. This also enabled completion of our Whitecastle initiative by allowing us to migrate the last AWS main account EMR cluster to a child account. Bonus: we simplified compliance by removing special security group configurations and the complex permission management that SSH access required. Operational Improvements Master node resource contention: eliminated. All non-Hadoop jobs now run in distributed YARN containers with proper resource allocation instead of competing for resources on the master node. Job reliability: dramatically improved. Jobs survive client Kubernetes pod restarts because Quarry maintains server-side job tracking. No more zombie processes. Jobs terminate properly when cancelled through REST APIs. We gained proper lifecycle management with clean cancellation and cleanup. Observability: transformed. Structured job status, logs, and metrics are now available through Quarry’s API. We can track jobs across their entire lifecycle, see YARN container logs, and actually debug issues with proper tooling instead of SSH-ing into boxes and hoping for the best. Future Enablement The REST-based architecture unblocked critical initiatives: Spark on Kubernetes migration now possible (no SSH dependencies to migrate) Modern infrastructure patterns enabled (REST-based architecture aligns with cloud-native practices) Easier team onboarding (simpler, more maintainable Quarry operators vs. complex SSH configurations) Platform evolution (decoupled Airflow from EMR infrastructure details) Standardized job submission (consolidated all job submission through Quarry, making future changes easier) With two years of production experience since completion, the architectural decisions have proven sound. The REST-based approach delivered on its promises: better security, operational stability, and infrastructure flexibility. No regrets. What We Learned What Worked Well Incremental migration approach: Dev → GovDev/CommDev → Prod rollout minimized risk at every step. We migrated jobs by operator type rather than trying to convert everything simultaneously. This allowed us to learn from each migration and refine our approach for the next batch. Strong team collaboration: Multiple teams working together seamlessly across search, analytics, data engineering, ML, and marketing domains. Prompt code reviews kept momentum high. Regular communication in shared channels kept everyone informed. Analytics-driven progress tracking: We created an Analytics dashboard to track migration progress across all regions. Querying the Airflow database to identify remaining SSH-based tasks made it easy to see which teams/DAGs still needed migration. This data-driven approach kept the project moving. What We’d Do Differently Earlier network topology mapping: We discovered network segregation issues (like the EKM connectivity problem) pretty late in the migration. Understanding Whitecastle account boundaries and network routing upfront would’ve saved us some pain. Next time: document network topology and dependencies before starting cluster migrations. Don’t assume SSH’s simplicity means everything will “Just Work” when you swap it out. Earlier resource limit testing: The vmem check issue caught us by surprise late in the project. We should’ve tested YARN resource limits against an SSH baseline way earlier in the process. Recommendation: Include resource limit testing in the initial pilot migration phase. SSH bypasses a lot of stuff, and you want to know what that stuff is before it bites you in production. Better communication about operator restrictions: When we restricted SSHOperator to prevent new usage during the final migration phase, some teams weren’t aware. Better advance notice to all Airflow users would’ve prevented confusion and friction. Internal communication is hard, but it matters. Best Practices for Large-Scale Migrations Build monitoring before you migrate: Set up tracking dashboards early so you always know what’s left to migrate. Airflow database queries made it easy to identify remaining work. Progress visibility kept the project moving. Test in multiple environments: Dev, CommDev, and GovDev testing caught environment-specific issues before production. Network segregation issues only appeared when testing across account boundaries. Don’t skip environment-specific testing. Hidden dependencies will absolutely bite you. Progressive operator deprecation: We deprecated operators one at a time (CrunchExecOperator, then S3SyncOperator, etc.). Each deprecation was its own mini-project with testing and validation. While it was slower than migrating everything at once, it greatly mitigated the risk of the migration. title: [Microsoft Azure] Evolving the cloud-native foundation for the next generation of AI
summary: Building a cloud-native foundation for AI The relationship between model innovation and AI infrastructure has never been more clear; as AI becomes more capable, the platform underneath it matters even more. Agents are fundamentally changing how applications work, and with that, what organizations need from the cloud. Learn how to build a cloud-native AI foundation Cloud-native practices gave organizations the scale, flexibility and resilience to build a generation of distributed applications. Agents build on that foundation, but they work differently, placing new demands on it. Unlike applications designed around more predictable workflows, agents behave in entirely new ways, gathering information and deep intelligence from across the business, using tools, making decisions, and coordinating work across long-running processes. To complete complex tasks, they pause for approval, respond to new information in real time and change course as conditions evolve. All this changes what the platform needs to deliver. Customers need infrastructure that adapts as demand changes, applications that remain reliable as work becomes more dynamic, and the visibility and control to understand what is happening across the system. Meeting those needs doesn’t mean starting over, but it does require that the cloud-native foundation organizations already rely on, to evolve. Compute, storage and networking need to work together. Application platforms need to make it easier to build and run AI workloads. Open technologies need to give customers flexibility without adding unnecessary complexity. The platform decisions organizations make today are increasingly strategic, shaping how effectively they can put AI to work for their business. Evolving the cloud-native foundation is essential to helping organizations get more from AI today while giving them the flexibility to take advantage of new capabilities as they emerge. Optimize infrastructure for AI workloads The true measure of AI infrastructure is the useful work it enables. AI workloads rarely place the same demands on infrastructure from beginning to end. Different parts of the work may need accelerated compute, CPUs, fast access to data or connectivity across applications and environments. The answer isn’t simply more capacity, but rather, to match the right resources to the right work at the right time. That makes coordination across the infrastructure extremely important. Compute, storage and networking need to work together as demands change. When they do, teams can spend less time managing infrastructure and more time focused on the applications and outcomes that matter to their business. Economics matter, too. Infrastructure needs to be tuned to the demands of the application and the business value it delivers, with the right balance of performance, reliability and cost across the complete workload. Basecamp Research is one example. In this example, AI didn’t simply require more infrastructure, it needed AI infrastructure that was coordinated and designed around the outcome – bringing together the compute, data and platform capabilities needed to move complex work forward. title: [Microsoft Azure] Infrastructure for the frontier era: Scaling intelligence through open industry collaboration
summary: At Microsoft, our vision is to build a Frontier Firm: one where people and technology work together, combining human expertise, context, and judgment with technology that can extend intelligence throughout everyday work. The potential is significant: helping people create, solve complex problems, and make progress on some of society’s most consequential challenges. But realizing that potential requires frontier infrastructure. The next phase of Super Intelligence needs a unified infrastructure engine that delivers more intelligence with greater efficiency, making AI more available, reliable, and sustainable across science, healthcare, education, and the economy. This is the work of an entire ecosystem, and precisely the vision we have advanced for years through our industry collaboration within the Open Compute Project Foundation. Designing silicon in the loop with real workloads As we enter the next phase of Super Intelligence, inference is becoming the dominant workload and that’s where efficiency, latency, and cost really matter. Azure Maia 300, our next generation AI accelerator from our Maia family, advances the inference efficiency frontier. Maia 300 is a complete system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences, and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks. By improving efficiency across the system, we expect Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per watt compared to leading GPU-based systems. And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to seven times the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200. Learn more about Maia 300 Maia reflects our system co-design approach. It is designed alongside Microsoft infrastructure and production workloads, bringing models, application frameworks, kernels, communication libraries, systems software, and custom silicon into one optimization loop. Maia 200 is deploying across the United States, Europe and Australia and delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for built-in AI capabilities in Microsoft Teams, Copilot and Cowork experiences compared with leading GPU infrastructure. Azure Maia 200 systems in a datacenter AI is not only about accelerators. Agentic workloads create entirely new demands on CPUs. Every agent interaction generates orchestration, data retrieval, memory management, and service calls that must occur quickly and efficiently. That is why we designed Cobalt 200 as an agent-native CPU. Cobalt 200 delivers more than 50% performance improvement over Cobalt 100 and reduces agent call latency by 33%, while providing 23% higher throughput on agentic workloads. Azure Cobalt 200 systems in a datacenter Maia and Cobalt are designed in the loop with our largest enterprise workloads. That gives Microsoft a unique advantage in tuning performance, reliability, and cost to exactly what customers need in production. We are applying the same principle to storage and security. The Azure Boost Data Processing Unit moves compression, networking transactions, and security functions away from the CPU onto purpose-built silicon, enabling us to deliver four times more performance while using significantly less power. And Azure Integrated HSM makes security part of the hardware foundation, with our in-house security chip in all new datacenter servers. It brings cryptographic operations closer to the workload while keeping keys protected inside the hardware security boundary—not exposed in application memory. Building an open, resilient AI fabric Compute creates intelligence and networks make it usable at scale. Working with industry partners, Microsoft developed Multipath Reliable Connection (MRC), rethinking Ethernet for AI. Its multi-plane architecture scales beyond 100,000 GPUs with two network tiers, reducing power, complexity, failure points, and cost. By intelligently distributing traffic across multiple paths and through packet spraying, MRC limits congestion and maintains reliable performance for frontier-scale training. We are also advancing open scale-up connectivity through Optical Compute Interconnect Multi-Source Agreement (OCI MSA). OCI, the first optical specification for multi-rack scale-up systems, enables high-bandwidth, power-efficient, multi-vendor infrastructure. Moving forward, we will continue to work with the industry to expand participation in OCI MSA. In parallel, The Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) workstream brings together more than 175 organizations to define requirements for Ethernet-based scale-up networking. The group has released specification version 1.0 and is developing version 1.1 for later this year. Read more about our networking innovations with the open community. Rethinking power from grid to silicon AI infrastructure is also forcing a fundamental redesign of power delivery. Through OCP and the Open Systems for AI initiative, Microsoft is helping advance the industry’s transition toward 800 volt direct current (VDC) infrastructure. Mt. Diablo, Microsoft’s disaggregated high-voltage datacenter (DC) sidecar architecture, separates power conversion from the compute rack so each can scale independently. It includes a modular design supporting approximately 100 kilowatts (kW) to beyond one megawatt (MW), with redundant feeds, telemetry and optional energy storage. Microsoft, together with OCP partners, contributed Mt. Diablo specifications v0.7 and v1.0 to OCP. Microsoft and its partners are advancing solid-state transformer-based architectures to make power conversion more efficient, responsive, and scalable for next-generation 800 VDC datacenters. Through OCP’s Clean Backup Power initiative, we are developing open requirements for reliable backup systems that reduce reliance on diesel. In parallel, Microsoft collaborated with partners to release a common grid-interface specification to align utilities, operators, and equipment vendors as hyperscale power architectures evolve. Read more about Microsoft’s approach to 800VDC transition and scaling power infrastructure sustainably. Cooling as a first-class design consideration Microsoft approaches cooling as a datacenter-wide challenge, driving innovation from DC facility design to rack-level liquid cooling technologies. Our third-generation Azure Heat Exchanger Unit, Mt. Atlas, nearly doubles cooling capacity compared to the previous generation while maintaining the same operational footprint. We are also contributing public reference architecture through OCP to help accelerate industry adoption. At the datacenter level, Microsoft is advancing a zonal cooling strategy in its next-generation AI datacenters to handle the growing mix of liquid-cooled accelerators and traditional air-cooled systems. By tailoring cooling to the specific needs of each workload, and introducing multiple independent water loops, each supplying coolant at different temperatures, we aim to increase efficiency and performance while supporting Microsoft’s energy, carbon, and water reduction goals. Open hardware security innovation Microsoft believes strong cloud security is built through openness, transparency, and industry collaboration. This principle is reflected in our founding role in the Confidential Computing Consortium, our work to establish Caliptra as an open-source silicon root of trust, and our contributions to the OCP S.A.F.E. security conformance framework. As AI reshapes the cybersecurity landscape and advances in quantum computing introduce new cryptographic risks, protecting the keys and credentials at the foundation of digital trust has never been more important. To address these challenges, and building on our commitment to security transparency and industry collaboration, Microsoft, Marvell, and Oracle are introducing Tessera Integrated HSM, an open-source initiative for integrated hardware security modules. Tessera Integrated HSM carries forward the workload direct attached HSM architecture introduced by Azure Integrated HSM, open-sourcing its architecture, specifications, protocols, drivers, software, firmware, and silicon to the broader community. Learn more about Tessera Integrated HSM. Fleet resiliency at scale As AI infrastructure scales, fleet reliability is essential to protecting customer workloads, capacity, and service quality. Through OCP, Microsoft has published common RAS, debugging, telemetry, and diagnostics specifications, while contributing work on hardware fault management, CPU and GPU management, and fleet memory fault management. We are using years of fleet data and using AI to validate, predict, and drive fleet actions aimed at preventing faults, pinpointing issues, and recovering more autonomously. Learn more about how Microsoft is advancing fleet reliability through industry collaboration. Advancing sustainability across the infrastructure stack Scaling AI responsibly means considering the full datacenter lifecycle to help reach our 2030 commitments to be carbon negative, water positive, and zero waste. As a company, we are committed to incorporating sustainability into how we design, build, and operate our datacenters extending to the communities where we build them. Through OCP, Microsoft is collaborating with partners on low-embodied-carbon steel and concrete—with pathways to reduce concrete emissions by more than 50% per cubic yard. We are advancing waste-heat reuse, and helping develop Cloud Services Product Category Rules for consistent, auditable lifecycle-carbon reporting. Inside our datacenters, closed-loop liquid cooling, intelligent power management, and renewable-energy agreements help reduce resource use, while Circular Centers reuse or recycle more than 90% of servers and components. Beyond the datacenter, we are investing in local skills, partnerships, and infrastructure so the communities hosting this growth can grow with us. Read Microsoft’s 2026 Environmental Sustainability report. Building the frontier together Our vision is to help every organization become a Frontier Firm, uniting human expertise with AI in a continuous learning loop that turns knowledge and ingenuity into scalable intelligence. Realizing that vision requires full-stack co-design: silicon, compute, memory, networking, power, cooling, models, and applications working as one secure, reliable, efficient, and sustainable platform while giving customers choice without passing complexity on to them. Such a future cannot be realized by a single organization. Through OCP, we are advancing open interfaces, sharing lessons from operating infrastructure at global scale, and collaborating across the industry so innovation moves faster, and the ecosystem stops solving the same problems repeatedly. Together, we can transform frontier innovation into infrastructure that makes intelligence accessible and affordable for every organization, in every industry, and across every region of the world. At OCP Global Summit 2026, we invite the community to build that future with us. Build for what’s next Learn more about Microsoft’s systems approach to infrastructure. title: [Docker] Manufacturing Trust for AI Agents | Docker’s WeAreDevelopers Keynote
summary: Coding agents do more than write code. Agents can install dependencies, access networks, use credentials, and keep working after we’ve moved on to something else. Agents need access to get real work done. But the more access they have, the bigger the impact of a mistake. The challenge is building enough trust into the system to give agents more freedom without giving them access to everything. At WeAreDevelopers North America, Docker President Mark Cavage laid out Docker’s answer: give every agent a strong boundary, make its environment and authority reproducible, and let the work run where it makes sense, from a developer’s laptop to the cloud. In 30 minutes, Mark demonstrates what happens when an agent pushes beyond a container’s limits and how Docker Sandboxes create a stronger boundary. He then connects that foundation to Kits, cloud capacity for work that needs to continue beyond the laptop, and new partnerships helping developers put agents to work safely. Agents are actors, not workloads Containers were built to isolate applications. Agents do more. They make decisions and act on the systems around them, so the boundary needs to extend to the environment they can reach. Mark’s onstage demo makes that clear. The container worked as designed. What the agent needed was containment around its full environment. Docker Sandboxes provide that containment. Each agent gets its own isolated microVM and kernel, separate from the developer’s host environment. Developers can choose the agent, model, and tools that fit the job, then define the sandbox’s access to files, networks, and secrets. Those policies stay outside the agent’s control. Together, the sandbox and its policies create a trusted environment for autonomous work. Docker Sandboxes are available today through the free, standalone CLI, so developers can bring stronger isolation to the agent workflows they already use. Make the agent and its authority reproducible A strong boundary gives an agent a safe place to work. Developers also need a repeatable way to define what runs and what it can access. In the keynote, Mark announced the next generation of Docker Sandbox Kits, now built as standard OCI images, and invited ecosystem partners to help shape the specification as Docker works towards neutral governance. Docker Sandbox Kits package the agent, its tools, and the rules for what the sandbox can reach into one versioned, shareable artifact. Developers can share Kits through the same workflows they already use for container images, while keeping changes to an agent’s authority visible and reviewable. The result is a common foundation for the agent ecosystem, built on an open standard. Dockerfiles made software reproducible. Kits make authority reproducible Start on your laptop. Finish in the cloud. Some agent work begins and ends on a developer laptop. Longer-running or parallel work needs capacity that stays available when the developer steps away. In the keynote, Mark announced Docker Cloud Sandboxes, bringing the same microVM-based isolation from the laptop to Docker-managed cloud compute. Using the familiar sbx workflow, developers can start locally, move their work to the cloud with one command, and let it continue after they close their laptop. They can also run tasks in parallel without provisioning or maintaining the infrastructure themselves. Docker Cloud Sandboxes are available today with pay-as-you-go pricing. An ecosystem built around trust An open agent ecosystem needs both: choice for the developers and shared standards the industry can build on. Nous Research joined Mark onstage to show Hermes running as a first-class Kit in Docker Sandboxes. The demo showed what choice looks like in practice: a third-party agent packaged for a common environment, with Docker providing the underlying isolation and controls. Developers can choose the agent that best fits their work without having to rebuild the trusted execution layer around it. Choice also depends on shared standards that the wider ecosystem can adopt. Docker has committed to submitting its Kits specification to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), the open source, vendor-neutral hub of cloud-native computing. “Standards are what let an ecosystem move fast without fragmenting, and few companies understand that better than Docker through their involvement in efforts like the OCI and CNCF. By delivering Sandbox Kits as standard OCI images, Docker is giving the industry an open, repeatable way to package an AI agent, its tools, and its guardrails as one artifact. OCI is the foundation the cloud native ecosystem is built on, so a standard for agents that builds on OCI reaches the whole ecosystem at once. The cloud native community looks forward to working with Docker to bring this work under neutral governance.” Chris Aniszczyk CTO at CNCF Together, these partners show what an open agent ecosystem can look like: choice at the agent layer and a shared format for packaging an agent’s environment and authority. Docker provides the trusted foundation underneath, whether agents run locally or in the cloud. Trust comes from the system around the agent Taken together, the announcements in Mark’s keynote form one system. Sandboxes provide a deterministic boundary. Kits make the agent’s environment and authority reproducible. Cloud Sandboxes extend the same trust model to durable cloud capability. They give developers the freedom to choose their agents and more autonomy, while retaining control over what they can access and change. As agents take on bigger jobs, the infrastructure around them matters more. Docker provides the trusted foundation they need to work locally or scale in the cloud, while developers continue to stay in control of what ships. Ready to try Cloud Sandboxes? For a limited time, new accounts can claim $250 in compute credit to get started. title: [Engineering at Meta] How Meta Built Forum With AI-Native Engineering
summary: Meta’s newest app, Forum, is for anyone who wants to go deeper into the conversations in their Facebook groups. To build Forum, Meta engineers adopted a whole new way of working by bringing an AI agent into the development cycle. We’re sharing insights into what it took to build Forum with agentic AI: how we adapted the codebase, tested frameworks and internal tooling for agentic execution, what worked, and what didn’t. Forum is a standalone Groups app that a small team built from scratch. It’s also where we tested a different way of working: treating an AI agent as a participant in the engineering process rather than a faster way to type. That experiment needed a definition of success, and ours wasn’t code volume. We measured verified, production-ready outcomes — changes that build, pass tests, and survive review. From Human-In-The-Loop to Human-On-The-Loop Pointing AI at the coding step alone doesn’t change much. Our results compounded as we extended the approach to the stages around implementation — planning, building, testing, and verification. The clearest way to see the shift is in who owns each step. With human-in-the-loop, the engineer drives every step and the AI assists inside it by autocompleting a function, suggesting a fix, or answering a question. Each iteration advances at the pace of the person driving it. With human-on-the-loop, the agent runs the iteration itself — plan, implement, build, test, correct, repeat — while the engineer sets the goal, watches the run, steps in when it drifts, and approves the result. The person’s job moves from executing the steps to owning the outcome and holding the quality bar. This is the target we are driving toward, not a finished state: some stages run autonomously today, while others still keep an engineer in each iteration. When the engineer supervises, work stops being strictly sequential. Cycles that used to run one at a time can overlap, and an engineer’s time goes to direction and judgment rather than to sitting through the loop. But that only holds if what comes back can be trusted. Without verification, AI-generated code creates a familiar problem — plausible output that no one has confirmed actually works, which an engineer then has to read, debug, and often discard. Weak signals don’t remove the constraint; they move it from writing code to reviewing code that looks finished and isn’t. So we set the bar at verification rather than compilation. Compiling isn’t the finish line — a task is complete only once automated tests and visual checks have passed. Agents check their own work before an engineer sees it, which means what reaches review is a smaller set of higher-confidence results rather than a pile of output to sift through. Less gets generated, and less gets discarded. Every shipped outcome still carries an engineer’s sign-off; our effort went into making that sign-off fast and well-evidenced, with build results, test outcomes, and recorded verification sessions attached to the change. With the engineer outside of every cycle, the loop has to run safely on its own. Four capabilities make that possible: Planning as technical specification: Agentic execution requires extreme precision. Ambiguity that an engineer might resolve through intuition results in agent failure. We invested in rigorous upstream decomposition and machine-readable context, which tightened the engineering loop for engineers and agents alike. Automated verification inside the loop is the force multiplier: We integrated automated pass/fail signals — build status, unit tests, and UI spec matching — directly into the agent loop. This enabled asynchronous development producing ready-to-review pull requests with pre-populated test plans and recorded verification sessions. Verification is the hard part to get right, and how much we can safely hand to the loop is gated by how much we can trust the verifiers. Simulated user testing with agents: We deployed navigation agents that interact with the live app exactly like a person would. These agents perform actions, read the screen, and report regressions. Navigation agents are able to run the same verification paths continuously. Agentic production operations: After launch, agents help automate root-cause analysis. When someone using Forum submits feedback, the agents use that feedback to investigate possible regressions. The agents then forward the analysis to engineers who decide the next course of action. The Operating Model That ownership model needs machinery with five key components: Rules are permanent project instructions. When the agent repeats a mistake more than twice, we encode the correction once, for everyone. Skills turn team conventions into loadable steps the agent can invoke. Agents automate checks that previously required a manual pass. Commands chain skills and agents into workflows. They assess complexity, reproduce a bug, plan and implement a fix, create the pull request, and run a multi-stage review. Hooks are automated triggers, such as running a linter after every agent turn, checking simulator connectivity before install, and validating tests before a pull request is created. Adapting the Environment to the Models The biggest gains came from changing our code and tooling, not our prompts. Architectural legibility over inherited complexity: We worked to keep Forum’s codebase as straightforward as possible and chose to modularize key pieces of the architecture in order to get the benefits of battle-tested infrastructure while also letting the agents plug and play easily. Where we couldn’t easily do so, we rebuilt from scratch, trading reuse for agentic throughput, and it proved rewarding in development speed. Agents learn patterns from the code they read. Fix a weak pattern once and every future agent session inherits the improvement; leave it and the same shortcut shows up in everything the agent writes next. Give agents tools, not descriptions: Our main failure mode was the agent losing track of where it was in the app — editing the home feed when asked to change the group home screen, or guessing at screen coordinates. So instead of describing the app to the agent, we gave it tools to check: read the live view hierarchy from the simulator, list the elements actually on screen, and look up the path to a target view — all before it acts. Misdirected edits dropped sharply. We applied the same approach wherever agents touched our systems: give the agent a way to check state directly rather than a description to reason from. Build-level isolation for safe AI prototyping: As Forum matured toward production, we wanted early-stage prototypes and agent-generated experiments to have room to run while keeping the production app strictly limited to finished, reviewed work. We wanted a stronger guarantee than feature gating alone, where prototype code still exists inside the production build. Our solution was a separate build flavor, a sandbox app that shares the exact same codebase, frameworks, and design system as production, but compiles prototype code out of the production build entirely via a plugin/socket architecture. This gave us three things at once: Designers and cross-functional partners could prototype freely using AI tools without needing an engineer in the loop for each change. Anything built in the sandbox could be ported directly to production with no rebuild. No prototype code could crash the production app because it physically didn’t exist in that build. The pattern let us keep fast AI iteration after we had real people using the app to protect. Finding Real Bugs With AI Stress Testing Adapting the environment did more than make the agent faster to build with — it made the agent a tester. We didn’t point it at one specific defect. Instead, we set up repeatable stress scenarios that mimic real user behavior (aggressive scrolling, random group browsing, rapid navigation, repeated media loading) and ran them routinely across builds. Because these runs produce consistent signals (crashes, memory growth, page faults, UI regressions), the agent can triage anomalies, narrow to the triggering sequence, and then investigate the root cause. One such run surfaced a memory issue. The agent isolated a repro, proposed a fix, and verified it — all during development, before the app reached users. The fix materially reduced on-device memory growth and page faults across repeated stress sessions. While engineers made the architectural decisions, the detection and regression monitoring were automated and repeatable; once an anomaly was detected, the agent could reproduce → isolate → propose a fix → verify with the same harness. Applying the Same Discipline to Forum’s Feed We applied the human-on-the-loop approach in two places: Building the stack: Agents mapped the architectural options and trade-offs; engineers then evaluated and chose. What we deliberately kept human was the target — deciding what a good outcome looks like is a product judgment, not something the system should define for itself. Operating the stack: Questions that used to require whichever engineer knew the relevant code path now go to an investigation agent that gathers what it needs and posts a write-up with suggested fixes. After hand-scoring a batch of real investigations we arrived at a workflow where the agent compresses the mechanical work and delivers a structured write-up to an engineer, who then validates whether a finding is a real bug or an intentional trade-off. What improved quality wasn’t better prompting. It was context. One recurring category of investigation came back weak until we gave the agent the same pointers to the relevant code, example queries, and design docs that we’d give any new engineer on day one. The quality of that category jumped. The difference from human onboarding is that you train once, and every future session starts from it. Did It Work? Beyond shipping faster, we shipped cleaner. Continuous verification surfaced systemic issues — like the memory bottleneck above — during development rather than after launch. The results show up in the performance profile: Quality, found early: The autonomous stress-testing loop caught and fixed the aforementioned memory issue during development rather than post-launch, roughly halving memory use and page faults. Velocity: Forum reached core feature parity with Facebook Groups in eight weeks, with AI handling much of the routine implementation so engineers could focus on architecture, product decisions, and quality. Leverage that lasted: After launch, agent-driven investigation helped engineers triage and root-cause user feedback. The AI did more than generate code. It tightened our quality loop, helping a small team deliver a high-quality app with less ongoing rework. What Worked, and What Did Not Acknowledgements We thank Neeharika Sinha, Jane Kou, Gang Yang, Guohao Zhang, Zeya Zhang, Kinnary Jangla, andYonghui Lu for their valuable contributions. title: [Engineering at Meta] 2026 World Cup: Breaking Records, Spiky Charts and Reliability at Scale
summary: Every four years, the World Cup becomes the largest planned stress test of our infrastructure. This year it also set an all-time record! There are a few moments throughout the year, like New Years Eve, that really let us see the collective impact of everything we’ve built — but none are bigger than the quadrennial World Cup tournament. The 2026 World Cup broke records across messaging, video, recommendations, and networking at the same time. Some highlights: WhatsApp: More than 30 million messages per second during the July 19 final (Argentina vs. Spain), 1.23x the peak of New Year’s Eve 2026 and an all-time platform record. The previous record had already fallen 12 days earlier, during the Round of 16 match between Argentina and Egypt, at 29 million messages per second. Messenger, Threads, and Instagram Direct: 49 million messages per minute at peak. Instagram: Recommendation system traffic up to 80% higher week-over-week. Final-squad players collectively added +213.6 million activated followers — a 6.6% increase — with combined followings surging from 3.26 billion to 3.47 billion. Live video: Watch time spiked +90% on Instagram and +242% on Facebook, versus the July baseline. Threads: 1.5 billion impressions on tournament-tagged posts, reaching about 15 million people daily and peaking at 25 million on July 6. Facebook: 80 million posts mentioning the World Cup. Traffic Followed the Breaks, Not the Ball Every World Cup match caused surges in traffic. During the final, for example, traffic surged +46% in about four minutes at the end of regular time, and +57% in about 15 minutes at the final whistle. But by lining game events up against global egress traffic we discovered a striking pattern – surges in sharing were primarily happening during breaks (hydration breaks, halftime, extra time, the final whistle, the awards ceremony). The end-of-regulation whistle produced the single biggest peak of the tournament. It wasn’t the gameplay that moved our charts. It was the conversations after it. The world came to Meta to watch the game and to share what it made them feel. Every capacity decision below follows from that one pattern. Layered Systems, No Manual Intervention Those spikes were absorbed by systems built for exactly this. Taiji balanced load across datacenters, Katran and Proxygen handled L4/L7 traffic distribution, our global load balancing system routed users to the best-positioned edge, and AutoScaling provisioned capacity on demand. Region-Specific Capacity Months before kickoff, Meta’s edge teams analyzed network capacity and worked closely with ISP partners so that upgrades landed where they would most improve quality of experience for end users. That targeted pre-build is now permanent capacity that will keep serving demand long after the tournament. Instagram: Preparing for 39 Consecutive Days of Surges For Instagram, the tournament meant 39 straight days of traffic spikes as billions of fans checked scores, posted Stories, and flooded Feed during breaks. Machine learning inference, Feed serving, Stories, Explore, and data infrastructure all had to absorb it without degrading the experience. During the final, halftime Instagram Feed traffic rose 76% above the previous day in the minute the match ended, and stayed about 21% above for the following two hours. Our approach rested on four things, deployed incrementally as the tournament moved from group stage to final. Capacity buffers: Our products went into the tournament with sufficient capacity, which meant real buffers were available to allocate. We pre-provisioned significant additional capacity across all serving tiers so that spikes never had to wait on autoscaling to catch up. These dedicated buffers were our single most effective lever of the tournament. Country-level graceful degradation: For high-risk matches, we shed non-critical background load in the top-traffic nations (Brazil, Argentina, India, Indonesia, Spain) to protect core functionality. Cascade prevention: So spikes at the serving layer couldn’t propagate into downstream data systems. Early warning signals These alerted us before we approached capacity thresholds, rather than after. All of this, including the phased deployment timeline and the degradation activation criteria, is now a reusable runbook for future large-scale events like the 2028 Olympics. WhatsApp: 8.4 Billion Messages in Five Minutes Goals and the final whistle drove WhatsApp spikes lasting four to five minutes at a time. In its single highest-traffic five-minute window, WhatsApp delivered nearly 8.4 billion messages without interruption. That came from months of preparation. More than 100 internal services were load-tested and resized ahead of the tournament, then retested, revalidated, and resized as the bracket narrowed and demand climbed. Two things we’d normally do, we didn’t. We didn’t shift load between regions. For past high-traffic events, our default has been to spread demand across multiple regions, letting capacity in quieter parts of the world absorb the spike. That works when peaks land hours apart — a global New Year’s Eve, for example. This event was different. Every region peaked in the same instant, so there was no idle capacity to borrow. Instead of deriving regional demand from a global multiplier, we forecast each region’s peak on its own terms. We didn’t freeze. The other standard playbook move for a major event is to pause continuous deployment and hold off on riskier operations like disaster recovery exercises. This time we skipped the freeze entirely, on the strength of years of reliability enhancement. Teams shipped on their normal cadence throughout the entire event window, including during the peak moment itself. We Stay Ready Year-Round Enabling connection in moments like this doesn’t just happen. Powering every message sent, every follower, and every Reel shared in real time across 48 teams and 104 matches is a story of infrastructure and product working as one. Capacity planning, load testing, traffic management, and rapid incident response come together across these teams so that billions of people can connect in the moments that matter most — like an entire continent celebrating a last-minute goal at the same second.
