title: [Engineering at Meta] OCP Summit 2026: Powering AI with Open Innovations in Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across Networks
summary: At the 2026 Open Compute Project Global Summit, Meta is sharing the next generation of open networking infrastructure, including: Our first liquid-cooled network rack (IcePack), and 102.4T switch platform (IceCube). Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF), a multiplane backend scale-out fabric that fundamentally changes how GPUs connect to the network MetaRoCE, our open-source AI transport protocol. Launching the Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) initiative within OCP. We’re inviting engineers, silicon vendors, system integrators, and operators to join us and the OCP community in meeting the challenges of building open, efficient, and sustainable AI infrastructure. At Meta, we believe that open networking is critical for building high-performance, scalable, and sustainable infrastructure, and we’ve acted on that conviction since co-founding the Open Compute Project (OCP) in 2011. Throughout the ongoing AI revolution, Meta has pushed the boundaries of what’s possible in data center networking and shared our advances with the industry. At OCP 2025, we introduced our latest AI scale-out fabrics and drove the creation of the Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) initiative. This year at OCP 2026, we’re sharing the networking innovations that directly support our latest AI workloads such as Meta’s Muse Wonder and Muse Spark models, and Muse, our personal AI agent built for everyone. Here’s some of what’s new: The 102.4T scale-out switch: Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack (IcePack) and 102.4T switch blades (IceCube), designed to support high power density, deliver higher thermal efficiency, and enable gigawatt-scale AI clusters. The scale-out Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF): Meta’s multiplane fabric, enabling larger, highly efficient GPU clusters with lower latency — with learnings shared with our cloud partners. Scale-across for multi-site clusters: Meta’s petabit-scale backend aggregation (BAG) super-spine and how large-scale training jobs deal with failures at this scale — with an overview of how we’ve built SRv6 regional backbones using FBOSS and SAI to handle even longer distances Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking: Meta’s MTIA 300 system uses Tahan, an Ethernet-based 51.2T scale-up switch, delivering 6.4 Tbps per accelerator — with a preview of next-gen 72-accelerator-per-rack design on 102.4T silicon and moving toward an ESUN-based implementation with future chips. Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA): a new OCP initiative, co-led by Meta, Microsoft, and Alibaba, that standardizes the switch platform layer — with specification v1.0 now submitted to OCP. MetaRoCE: Meta’s RDMA transport protocol for AI networks — now with open-source implementations. The 102.4T Generation: Liquid-Cooled Networking at AI Scale As AI clusters grow to gigawatt scale, network switches must deliver dramatically more bandwidth while fitting within increasingly dense power and cooling envelopes. Our answer is the IcePack rack, Meta’s first-generation liquid-cooled network rack. IcePack is based on OCP’s ORV3-HPRv1 rack standard. IceCube switch blades — 102.4-Tbps fabric switches that deliver 128×800G non-blocking switching capacity — sit inside each rack. IceCube comes in two variants, one built on Broadcom’s Tomahawk6C switch ASIC and one on NVIDIA Spectrum-6 Switch ASIC. Both run Meta’s open-source FBOSS network operating system that leverages OCP SAI (Switch Abstraction Interface). This new generation represents a 2x bandwidth increase over our 51.2T platforms while achieving the thermal density required for next-generation AI data centers. The IcePack rack — Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack, populated with IceCube 102T switch blades. IceCube — Meta’s 102.4 Tbps liquid-cooled switch blade, delivering 128×800G non-blocking capacity and running FBOSS. Scaling AI Fabrics From Building to Region As seen at Meta and across the industry, AI clusters now span buildings, campuses, and multiple regions. This demands fabric architectures that are not only massive in scale but also resilient and flexible. Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF): More Resilient, Larger Clusters We’re introducing Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF), Meta’s multiplane backend scale-out fabric that fundamentally changes how GPUs connect to the network and the network control plane of the fabric. With FPF, each GPU connects via eight independent 100G links to eight different switches (one per network plane). This multiplane approach replaces the traditional single-plane uplink architecture and delivers four key advantages: Larger non-blocking GPU clusters compared to single-plane topologies, which enables the scale required for our largest AI training workloads A flattened topology, moving from the 3-tier Clos fabric of our NSF fabric to a 2-tier Clos fabric. Removing this tier of switches reduces network hops, latency, and infrastructure cost. NIC-level hardware load balancing: Load balancing, traditionally done by network switches, now starts at the NIC, which sprays every packet across all eight planes in hardware. A combined control plane for fault tolerance: The control plane of FPF includes both the switches and the hosts, allowing the host to steer traffic away from downed planes. Meta collaborated closely with NVIDIA on developing FPF running inside Meta’s infrastructure, leveraging NVIDIA Spectrum-X Multiplane innovations to ensure FPF has high performance even under assorted failure conditions and operational lifecycle scenarios. Going beyond our own infrastructure, Meta and NVIDIA have been working closely with our joint cloud partners to help standardize multiplane fabrics implementations within those partners based on our FPF learnings. Bridging On-Prem Data Centers and Public Cloud This work with cloud providers on FPF is just one example of how we at Meta are not just building our own infrastructure, but are helping our partners’ infrastructure. Our ambitions for scaling our AI capacity cannot be met by building data centers alone, because construction runs on multi-year lead times while demand moves in months. So we use leased facilities and public cloud capacity, alongside our own campuses, to close the gap. But it only works if the network behaves the same way no matter where the GPUs sit. That is genuinely difficult, because cloud networking is not the same as owning the rack. Fabric topologies differ from provider to provider rather than following one uniform design. Buffering is often shallower, which changes congestion and loss behavior. RDMA transports are provider-specific, and some clouds still run InfiniBand rather than Ethernet and RoCE. What works for a handful of cloud instances also tends to break at fleet scale. At OCP we’re sharing how we’re converging these environments into a single operational model. That includes a standardized performance validation framework — cloud partners run a common suite of point-to-point and collective benchmarks, scaling from tens to over a thousand GPUs, before a cluster is ever handed over, so performance is proven rather than assumed. It includes normalizing heterogeneous, often multiplane fabrics, mapping divergent traffic-class schemes and congestion-control parameters onto our lossless RDMA classes so end-to-end paths behave predictably across different vendors’ NICs and switches. The principle we keep applying is that heterogeneity is manageable but standardization is what makes it affordable. Testing and qualification, RDMA transport and congestion behavior, and telemetry all still diverge across providers, and every divergence becomes engineering work. BAG: Scale-Across Aggregation The scale of AI capacity Meta has committed to this decade — Prometheus at roughly 1 gigawatt in 2026, and Hyperion scaling toward 5 gigawatts— means a single cluster now outgrows any single region. Our backend aggregation (BAG) layer is a centralized, Ethernet-based super-spine that interconnects many spine-layer fabrics into one mega cluster spanning buildings, campuses, and regions. It operates at petabit scale — inter-BAG capacity between a pair of regions reaches tens of petabits per second. BAG is what allows Prometheus to function as a single cluster even though its capacity is spread across conventional data center buildings, weatherproof outdoor structures, and adjacent colocation space. At this reach, distance itself becomes a design constraint. Lossless Ethernet requires buffer headroom proportional to cable length, so once links stretch tens of kilometers, buffer management turns into a first-order problem rather than a tuning detail. And getting it wrong risks congestion spreading well beyond the link that caused it. Instead of provisioning every link for a worst-case distance, FBOSS now measures actual cable length in place, timing probe traffic on an uncongested queue to derive round-trip distance, and allocates headroom against the measurement. Load balancing also has to reason about paths that are degraded rather than simply down. BAG uses eBGP link-bandwidth signaling so traffic is distributed in proportion to the capacity actually available on each path, with deliberate damping so that a single link failure does not ripple routing churn across the domain. And because inter-fabric latency is several times intra-fabric latency, collective communication libraries — which generally choose algorithms without any awareness of network distance — can fall off a performance cliff. We’ve been addressing that from both directions, with adaptive routing improvements to reduce the latency penalty and scheduling that minimizes how much collective traffic needs to cross the BAG layer at all. Training remains resilient throughout. When a replica fails, it is automatically excluded and the surviving replicas continue synchronizing across BAG. The direction of travel is longer distances still — training jobs spanning regions tens, hundreds, or thousands of kilometers apart — and increasingly heterogeneous clusters that mix hardware generations and vendors. Backend aggregation (BAG) connects building-scale AI fabrics — both DSF and NSF — across sub-regions into a unified training network. SRv6-Powered Regional Backbone Using FBOSS We’ve deployed Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) using FBOSS for our regional backbone networks. This enables more flexible traffic engineering and simplified operations as we interconnect AI clusters across geographies — running on open shallow-buffer switch platforms powered by Cisco SiliconOne, with ongoing work to onboard additional silicon families, all managed under FBOSS using OCP SAI. Meta’s Regional Backbone (RBB) interconnects data center campuses and bridges to public cloud capacity. Ethernet for Scale-Up: Our Commitment to Ethernet A defining milestone of OCP 2026 is proving that Ethernet can serve the scale-up domain — the high-bandwidth, ultra-low-latency interconnects between accelerators within a rack or pod that have traditionally required proprietary technologies. Tahan: Ethernet-Based Scale-Up Switch We’re introducing Tahan, Meta’s Ethernet-based scale-up switch — purpose-built for our MTIA 300 training accelerators. Tahan is built on the 51.2 Tbps Tomahawk 5 ASIC from Broadcom, offering total capacity of 64x800G, half of which is used to provide scale-up connectivity to the accelerators via the backplane. Four Tahan switches interconnect 16 accelerators in a non-blocking topology. Importantly, Tahan reuses the same lossless RoCE transport (routed IPv6, PFC, AI-tuned QoS) as our scale-out network, unifying both scale-up and scale-out fabrics under FBOSS. Tahan, Meta’s first open, Ethernet-based scale-up switch (32×800G), liquid-cooled and running FBOSS. Next-Generation Scale-Up: 72 Accelerators per Rack on 102.4T Silicon We’re also previewing the next-generation scale-up blade, a 216×400G switch built on 102.4 Tbps Broadcom Tomahawk6C silicon. Eight of these switches interconnect 72 accelerators per rack, a dramatic increase in density enabled by the bandwidth of the 102.4T generation. A future generation of this scale-up blade is planned to adopt OCP Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) as the scale-up data plane, cementing our commitment to open standards for the entire scale-up stack. The next-generation MTIA scale-up blade: 216×400G on 102.4 Tbps silicon, adopting OCP ESUN as the scale-up data plane. ESUN Evolving The ESUN initiative we founded within OCP last year has made significant progress. Working alongside AMD, Arista, ARM, Broadcom, Cisco, HPE, Marvell, Microsoft, and NVIDIA, ESUN is advancing open specifications for: Protocol headers and framing optimized for scale-up topologies. Error handling mechanisms for lossless multi-hop fabrics. Alignment with UEC and IEEE standards. This work has already produced a concrete result with the ESUN 1.0 Network Operator Requirements Base Specification released earlier this year. ESUN 1.0 deliberately focuses on the fabric, defining what the network must deliver while leaving implementation flexibility to GPU and accelerator vendors, which broadens adoption. It also coordinates with existing standards bodies, leveraging work underway in IEEE and the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) rather than duplicating it. Since publishing ESUN 1.0, the group is now close to the next version, ESUN 1.1, tackling new features such as switch profiles and inter-packet gap reduction that further optimize Ethernet for low-latency, scale-up use cases. ESUN’s technical focus: a fabric-centric scope that preserves GPU implementation flexibility, coordinated with IEEE and UEC standards work with the ESUN 1.0 specification already released. With Tahan shipping today, a 72-accelerator-per-rack design on the horizon adopting ESUN as its data plane, and ESUN continuing to evolve its open specifications, we’re helping build a complete open platform for the scale-up future. Ecosystem Enablement and Open Transport Our commitment to openness extends across the full networking stack — from switch platform hardware to transport protocols. OSPA: Open Switch Platform Architecture SAI made switch data plane software portable across silicon. But the layer beneath it, the switch platform layer, has remained proprietary and fragmented. Every new hardware platform requires months of duplicated, custom engineering to bring up, and a lack of standard platform design multiplies long-term maintenance and troubleshooting cost. In an era of compressed AI hardware cycles, that onboarding tax has become untenable. To fix this, we’re co-leading a new OCP initiative with Microsoft and Alibaba, the Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) — a unified reference design for the switch platform layer. OSPA standardizes the hardware and software interfaces for: Power management and power sequencing. Sensor and environment control, including thermal and fan management. Hardware inventory management and device enumeration. Out-of-band hardware interfaces (management Ethernet, serial console, USB, LED indicators). Firmware maintenance and updates. Platform troubleshooting and diagnostics. FBOSS Ecosystem Enablement Over the past year we made a major push to extend open-source FBOSS so that switch vendors can self-onboard their own platforms without Meta engineers in the loop for the port. The goal is a self-service model in which multiple new switch platforms can be developed concurrently, giving vendors access to a hyperscale-proven NOS as they build FBOSS-compatible hardware. Vendors and developers can get started at the FBOSS documentation site and the FBOSS GitHub repository. MetaRoCE: Open-Source Transport for AI Clusters As we recently announced, MetaRoCE is our open-source RDMA transport protocol optimized for AI cluster networks over Ethernet. MetaRoCE provides the congestion control and reliability semantics that distributed AI training workloads demand. It’s purpose-built for the unique traffic patterns of collective communication across large-scale Ethernet fabrics. At OCP, we are announcing our open-source MetaRoCE implementations, enabling the broader AI infrastructure community to adopt and build upon a production-proven transport stack. Join Us in Building the Open Future of AI Networking The pace of AI infrastructure evolution continues to accelerate. The challenges of building open, efficient, and sustainable AI networking are too large for any single company to solve alone. We invite engineers, silicon vendors, system integrators, and operators to join us and the OCP community in defining what comes next. Visit our presentations at OCP 2026, explore our open-source contributions including FBOSS and MetaRoCE, and collaborate with us on building the networking infrastructure the AI era demands. The authors are members of the Network Infrastructure team at Meta. The post OCP Summit 2026: Powering AI with Open Innovations in Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across Networks appeared first on Engineering at Meta.

title: [Kubernetes] The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know
summary:
In Linux, cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources. Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers, ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other. With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into maintenance mode. Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25. Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy, a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation and modern resource-management features. Deprecation of cgroup v1Kubernetes has deprecated cgroup v1. Starting with Kubernetes v1.35, failCgroupV1 defaults to true, so the kubelet does not start on a cgroup v1 node by default. Administrators can temporarily set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration file, but removal will follow the Kubernetes deprecation policy. Further removal work is tracked in KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support. If you are still on a release older than v1.35, migrate every Linux node to cgroup v2 before upgrading, or plan to set the temporary failCgroupV1: false override. If you are already on v1.35 or later, confirm that every Linux node runs cgroup v2 (or that you intentionally keep the override). Under the default configuration, a remaining cgroup v1 node fails during kubelet startup. For kubeadm-managed clusters, Kubernetes v1.35 also makes this an earlier, stricter check. The SystemVerification preflight check, provided by k8s.io/system-validators, returns an error during kubeadm init, kubeadm join, and kubeadm upgrade when it detects cgroup v1 with kubelet v1.35 or later; with an older kubelet, the check remains a warning. See kubernetes/system-validators#1.12.1 release notes for details. The top FAQs cover three main areas: why to migrate, the benefits and drawbacks, and key points to keep in mind when using cgroup v2. Limitations of cgroup v1 and Improvements with cgroup v2The Linux kernel documentation describes both interfaces: cgroup v1 documentation cgroup v2 documentation Let's enumerate some known issues. active_file memory is not considered available memoryThe kubelet treats active_file memory as not reclaimable. For I/O-intensive workloads, a large page cache can therefore make the kubelet report memory pressure and evict Pods. This is a known kubelet issue (kubernetes/kubernetes#43916); migrating to cgroup v2 does not by itself change that calculation. The documented workaround is to set equal memory requests and limits for containers that perform intensive I/O, after measuring an appropriate value. Memory QoS updates in Kubernetes v1.36Memory QoS was introduced as an alpha feature in Kubernetes v1.22 and updated in v1.27. It remains alpha in v1.36, but now separates memory throttling from memory reservation and adds tiered memory protection: Memory QoS is available only on Linux nodes that use cgroup v2. It relies on the cgroup v2 memory controller: memory.high provides throttling, while memory.min and memory.low provide hard and soft protection when tiered reservation is enabled. cgroup v1 cannot provide this protection model. Enabling the MemoryQoS feature gate applies memory.high throttling to Burstable containers. The threshold is derived from the request, limit, and memoryThrottlingFactor (default 0.9). memoryReservationPolicy: None is the default. It does not write memory.min or memory.low. memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation maps Guaranteed Pod memory requests to memory.min (hard protection) and Burstable Pod requests to memory.low (soft protection). BestEffort Pods receive neither protection. The kubelet exposes Alpha metrics for the total memory.min and memory.low reservations on a node. Kernel 5.9 or later is recommended. On older kernels, memory.high reclaim can trigger a known livelock; from v1.36 the kubelet logs a warning when Memory QoS is enabled on an affected kernel. For example, to opt in to tiered protection: apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: KubeletConfiguration featureGates: MemoryQoS: true memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation memoryThrottlingFactor: 0.9 The overall Kubernetes recommendation is not to enable Alpha features in production; however, if you judge that memory QoS with tiered reservations is useful for your platform in production, make sure to test the configuration and account for hard-reserved memory before you enable the TieredReservation feature gate. See the Pod QoS documentation for the current mapping of Kubernetes QoS classes to cgroup v2 controls. Container-aware OOM handlingOn cgroup v2 nodes, the kubelet defaults singleProcessOOMKill to false. It therefore sets memory.oom.group for each container cgroup so that an OOM event kills all processes in that container together, rather than leaving a partially functioning multi-process container. Set singleProcessOOMKill: true only if you need the cgroup v1-compatible behavior where the kernel may kill one process at a time. See the KubeletConfiguration reference for this setting. This behavior is scoped to a container cgroup, not the whole Pod. Also, cgroup.kill is a separate administrative interface: writing 1 to it sends SIGKILL to every process in that cgroup and its descendants; it does not configure OOM behavior. The cgroup v2 memory controller additionally provides memory.events counters that monitoring systems and userspace OOM managers can observe. Rootless supportIn cgroup v1, delegating controllers to less privileged containers may be dangerous. Unlike cgroup v1, cgroup v2 officially supports delegation. Most implementations of rootless containers rely on systemd for delegating v2 controllers to non-root users. This delegation mechanism is separate from Kubernetes Pod user namespaces, which map container users to unprivileged host users. Pod user namespace support graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.36; check its filesystem, kernel, CRI runtime, and OCI runtime prerequisites before enabling it. What else? eBPF stories: In cgroup v1, device access controls are exposed through interface files. The cgroup v2 device controller has no interface files, and is implemented on top of cgroup BPF. Cilium attaches BPF cgroup programs for socket-based load balancing. Its default cgroup root is /run/cilium/cgroupv2. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) reports CPU, memory, and I/O contention at node, Pod, and container level. On supported clusters, the kubelet exposes PSI by default (KubeletPSI is stable and locked on). PSI requires cgroup v2, Linux 4.20 or later, CONFIG_PSI=y, and a kernel not booted with psi=0. The kubelet surfaces the data through the Summary API and /metrics/cadvisor. When migrating, update software that reads the cgroup filesystem directly. The migration guidance recommends cAdvisor v0.43.0 or later and lists compatible Java, Node.js, and automaxprocs versions. CPU weight conversion in newer OCI runtimescgroup v1 uses cpu.shares, whereas cgroup v2 uses cpu.weight. Newer OCI runtimes use an improved non-linear conversion that preserves the default priority and gives small CPU requests more usable granularity. The change is implemented in the OCI runtime rather than Kubernetes: it is available in crun v1.23 and runc v1.3.2. After upgrading a runtime, monitoring or policy tools that predict exact cpu.weight values may need updates. Read New Conversion from cgroup v1 CPU Shares to v2 CPU Weight for the formula, examples, and compatibility considerations. In-place resource updatesIn-place Pod vertical scaling graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.35. Kubernetes v1.36 then  (/blog/2026/04/30/kubernetes-v1-36-inplace-pod-level-resources-beta/) in-place vertical scaling for Pod-level resources by default, as a Beta feature. The kubelet coordinates changes between the Pod-level and container cgroups so that increases create headroom before container limits grow, while decreases constrain containers before shrinking the Pod-level boundary. Accurate aggregate enforcement for this v1.36 feature requires cgroup v2. Adopting cgroup version 2RequirementsHere's what you need to use cgroup v2 with Kubernetes. First up, you need to be using a version of Kubernetes with support for v2 cgroup management; that's been stable since Kubernetes v1.25 and all supported Kubernetes releases include this support. You need at least one Linux node; cgroup is a Linux-only concept Your OS install must run with cgroup v2 enabled The kernel version must be 5.8 or later (5.9 or later is recommended when using memory QoS) The container runtime must support cgroup v2. For example: containerd v1.4 or later supports cgroup v2; use containerd v2.0 or later for automatic cgroup-driver discovery CRI-O v1.20 or later The kubelet and the container runtime must both be configured to use the correct cgroup driver. See Configure the kubelet's cgroup driver to match the container runtime cgroup driver. For now, you can opt back in to use cgroup v1; the Kubernetes project recommends using cgroup v2, but in Kubernetes 1.36 (the current release) the cgroup v1 option remains supported as a fallback. That fallback is scheduled for removal in Kubernetes v1.38. If you are running an older cluster, plan to migrate; if you are setting up a new cluster with Linux nodes, you should prefer cgroup v2. In either case, review both the Kubernetes runtime documentation and (if relevant) the containerd compatibility matrix. kernel updates around cgroup v2When Kubernetes was first announced, in 2014, only v1 cgroup existed. Version 2 cgroup management first appeared in Linux kernel 4.5, released in 2016. In Linux 4.5, the cgroup v2 io, memory, and pids controllers were supported. Linux 4.15 added support for the cgroup v2 cpu controller. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) support began with Linux 4.20. The Kubernetes project does not recommend using cgroup v2 with a Linux kernel older than 5.2 due to lack of cgroup-level task freezer support. Kubernetes documents 5.8 as the minimum kernel version for cgroup v2; the root cgroup's system-level cpu.stat file was added in Linux 5.8. The memory.high livelock fix used by Memory QoS is present in Linux 5.9 and later. memory.peak was added in Linux 5.19. cgroup driver configurationConfigure the kubelet's cgroup driver to match the container runtime cgroup driver. If you use kubeadm to manage your cluster, Kubernetes recommends that you use the systemd cgroup driver, because kubeadm manages the kubelet as a systemd service. For other management tooling, check the documentation for the tool you're using to manage your cluster. If you can pick either option, I recommend using the systemd driver. Whatever tooling you've chosen, the kubelet automatically tries to detect the runtime's recommended cgroup driver. This automatic detection relies on using a runtime that implements the RuntimeConfig CRI RPC (for example: containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+). If you're using a container runtime that supports cgroup v2 but doesn't support automatic cgroup driver detection, you can manually configure an override by editing the kubelet configuration file. For example: apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: KubeletConfiguration cgroupDriver: systemd Automatic discovery of the runtime's cgroup driver through the CRI, tracked by KEP-4033, graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.34. It requires a runtime that implements the RuntimeConfig CRI RPC (containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+). When available, the kubelet uses the value reported by the runtime instead of its configured cgroupDriver value. Tools and commands for troubleshootingTools and commands that you should know about cgroups: stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup/: Check whether cgroup v2 is enabled; it returns cgroup2fs. systemctl list-units 'kube*' --type=slice or --type=scope: List Kubernetes-related units that systemd currently has in memory. bpftool cgroup list /sys/fs/cgroup/*: List all programs attached to the cgroup CGROUP. systemd-cgls /sys/fs/cgroup/*: Recursively show control group contents. systemd-cgtop: Show top control groups by their resource usage. tree -L 2 -d /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice: Show Pods' related cgroups directories. How to check if a Pod CPU or memory limit is successfully applied to the cgroup file?Work from the API object down to the node. Identify the node, then compare desired resources in the spec with the enacted values in status (in-place resize can leave those out of sync): kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}{"
"}' kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{range .spec.containers}{.name}{" spec	"}{.resources}{"
"}{end}' kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{range .status.containerStatuses}{.name}{" status	"}{.resources}{"
"}{end}' On that node, as root, with the systemd cgroup driver and cgroup v2 (these snippets also need jq). Pin the container with kubelet labels; a container name alone is not unique on a node. Use crictl ps -a if the container is not running: CONTAINER_ID=$(crictl ps \ --label io.kubernetes.pod.namespace=<namespace> \ --label io.kubernetes.pod.name=<pod-name> \ --name <container-name> -q | head -n1) # OCI view (not the CRI protobuf field names) crictl inspect "$CONTAINER_ID" | jq '.info.runtimeSpec.linux.resources' # Kernel cgroup path for this container PID=$(crictl inspect "$CONTAINER_ID" | jq -r '.info.pid') CGROUP="/sys/fs/cgroup$(awk -F: '$1=="0"{print $3}' /proc/$PID/cgroup)" cat "$CGROUP/cpu.weight" # request.cpu → shares → weight; not a limit cat "$CGROUP/cpu.max" # limit.cpu as "quota period"; unlimited is "max <period>" cat "$CGROUP/memory.max" # limit.memory; unlimited is "max" # Pod-level cgroup (parent slice), used by Pod-level resources cat "$(dirname "$CGROUP")/cpu.max" "$(dirname "$CGROUP")/memory.max" # Present when MemoryQoS is enabled cat "$CGROUP/memory.high" "$CGROUP/memory.min" "$CGROUP/memory.low" SCOPE=$(basename "$CGROUP") systemctl show "$SCOPE" \ -p CPUWeight -p CPUQuotaPerSecUSec -p CPUQuotaPeriodUSec -p MemoryMax Do not treat info.runtimeSpec.linux.cgroupsPath as a filesystem path when the runtime uses the systemd driver; that value is a systemd unit path (slice:runtime:id), not a directory under /sys/fs/cgroup. Expected mapping at each layer: Kubernetes: spec.containers.resources (desired) and status.containerStatuses.resources (enacted after in-place resize). Pod-level resources are on spec.resources and the parent pod slice. CRI (kubelet → runtime; these protobuf names stay cgroup v1-style even on v2): cpu_shares, cpu_quota, cpu_period, memory_limit_in_bytes, plus unified for Memory QoS. crictl inspect does not show these names; it shows the OCI spec the runtime derived from them. OCI spec: linux.resources.cpu.{shares,quota,period}, linux.resources.memory.limit, and linux.resources.unified. The runtime converts shares, quota, and period into cgroup v2 files. After upgrading crun or runc, the shares-to-weight formula may change; see CPU weight conversion. systemd scope: CPUWeight, CPUQuotaPerSecUSec, CPUQuotaPeriodUSec, MemoryMax. Unlimited or unset values often appear as  or infinity. cgroupfs: cpu.weight (from CPU request; an unset request still yields the default of 2 shares), cpu.max, and memory.max on the container scope. Memory QoS adds memory.high, memory.min, and memory.low. title: [Cloudflare] A fully programmable secure web gateway
summary: Every secure web gateway on the market works the same way: traffic matches a condition. A terminal action fires. Allow, Block, Isolate, Log. This model has been the foundation of network security for nearly 30 years, and it handles the common case well. But it has a ceiling, and customers with complex environments hit that ceiling regularly.Earlier this year, we shared our vision to build a truly programmable SASE platform. We also outlined how the term programmability has become diluted by the security industry. Most vendors claim programmability because they have public APIs, Terraform providers, webhooks, and alerting. Cloudflare offers all of those things too, but that’s not enough. True programmability means running your own code — arbitrary logic that you wrote for your specific environment — inline in the policy evaluation path, at the moment a security decision is made.Today, we’re excited to announce Cloudflare is bringing true programmability to Cloudflare Gateway and DLP (Data Loss Prevention) by integrating it with the entirety of our edge computing platform. We are releasing a new type of Gateway action, Forward, and custom validation functions, available to all Zero Trust plans. These capabilities allow you to use a Cloudflare Worker to transform and manipulate traffic, or to bring your own data to policy evaluation.The trade-off that every security team facesFor as long as firewalls have existed, businesses have faced a binary choice. You can maintain your own security detection engine — your own firewall, your own proxy infrastructure — with high maintenance overhead and low portability, in exchange for maximum customization. Or, you can accept the constraints of a vendor, offloading the considerable maintenance cost, at the expense of flexibility to solve problems specific to your environment.In six years of building Cloudflare Gateway, we have heard from thousands of customers struggling with this trade-off. A security team migrating access controls for a critical internal application needs to inject HTTP headers based on JSON Web Token (JWT) claims from their identity provider. The data exists in the request context, but Gateway cannot read the JWT and write the header. So the team stands up a pool of NGINX proxies solely to perform this transformation. That infrastructure now must be patched, monitored, and secured... indefinitely.Another team wants a Slack notification the moment an employee signs up for a new SaaS service. The policy engine can detect the sign-up event, but it can only Allow or Block. So the team builds a Logpush-to-SIEM-to-Slack pipeline with a 5 to 15 minute delay and no guarantee of delivery. And piles on yet another piece of infrastructure.Dozens of enterprise customers have asked for warning pages that prompt users for justification before allowing access to sensitive destinations. Most then want to customize the ensuing behavior based on additional context about who the user is and the level of access requested. But serving customized, dynamic responses from a policy engine is exceedingly difficult.We have offered customers many extension points over the years. But along with every other firewall vendor, it is impossible to build features to cover threat vectors as quickly as they can appear. However, we also recognize that the best solutions are those which are infinitely extensible to your environment.Why only Cloudflare can solve this problemCloudflare is not just a firewall, or a secure web gateway, a content delivery network, or an edge service. Cloudflare is a composable compute platform. Cloudflare Workers already allows customers to run complex logic on our network edge from any of our 330+ locations worldwide. Cloudflare Gateway already evaluates and enforces security policy on user traffic at those same locations, on the same machines, in the same data centers.Only Cloudflare runs both distributed customer compute and a full-featured secure web gateway and firewall in the same globally distributed network. We have the unique opportunity and ability to combine those functions into the industry’s first completely programmable and customizable SASE platform.Gateway and Workers were built on the same infrastructure from the beginning. When Gateway forwards traffic to a Worker, that dispatch is a local function call. There is no hairpinning. There is no additional latency from crossing a network boundary. This is the first time that customers will have absolute control over how their proxied traffic is processed, without compromise, using code that they can write and execute without maintaining any sort of infrastructure.Standalone SASE providers without their own compute platform require you to deploy automation in a separate cloud, manually configure webhooks, and accept the round-trip latency and management overhead of stitching together disconnected systems. No other vendor in this space has a programmable edge compute platform co-located with their security gateway. As threats advance at AI-powered speed, this will provide much needed flexibility and agility for security organizations.Two Gateway entry points: Forward action and Custom FunctionsA new Gateway action type called Forward and a new policy resource called a Custom Function are two distinct ways to call a Worker from a Gateway policy. The Forward action is available in public beta today, and Custom Functions will be available before the end of the year.Forward action: traffic transformation and proxyYou can customize HTTP traffic behavior with a new policy action called Forward that routes the matched HTTP request to a Worker as a proxy. Policies with the Forward action are evaluated for traffic allowed by HTTP policies. The first matching Forward rule will then be applied to your traffic, and the traffic will be sent to its bound Cloudflare Worker. The Worker acts as inline middleware: it receives the full headers and request body. Your logic can then choose to modify either one (or take another asynchronous action of some kind), forward the request to the origin, receive the response, can modify that too, and return the final response to the user.import { WorkerEntrypoint } from "cloudflare:workers"; import type { GatewayMiddlewareContext, GatewayMiddlewareNext, } from "@cloudflare/zt-types"; export class GatewayMiddleware extends WorkerEntrypoint { async handle( request: Request, context: GatewayMiddlewareContext, next: GatewayMiddlewareNext, ): Promise<Response> { // Read a value from the Gateway context const clientIP = context.srcIp; // Add headers before the request reaches the origin request.headers.set("X-Gateway-Client-IP", clientIP); // Forward upstream and get the response const response = await next(request); // Modify the response before it reaches the user response.headers.set("X-Processed-By", "gateway-middleware"); return response; } }Gateway handles the TCP connections, TLS termination and re-encryption, certificate management, and HTTP version negotiation. The Worker is responsible only for the transformation logic. You get a customizable, proxy-like extension point for your existing security stack, with none of the operational cost of hosting a traditional HTTP proxy.Your Workers also do not have to transform the request. A rule's sole purpose can be to proxy a request to a Worker that receives the full context of the matched request asynchronously: send a Slack message, write to R2, log to an external pipeline, call a webhook, update a KV store. The traffic can continue to its destination, unbothered.Custom functions: inline policy evaluationA custom function calls out to a Worker inline during Gateway policy evaluation and returns a value. The function is then exposed as a selector in the Gateway policy builder, and the selector is evaluated against its values. The selector is usable in the condition of any network or HTTP Gateway rule, the same way a built-in selector like Source IP or Content Category works today.The Worker receives context about the request: source IP, destination, user identity, device posture, HTTP headers, and more, depending on the policy phase. The Worker returns a typed value (string, number, or boolean) that Gateway uses in rule conditions. The contract is simple: data in, value out.Here is a custom function that parses a JWT Authorization header and returns the user's role:export class GatewayCustomSelector extends WorkerEntrypoint { async compute(ctx: GatewayContext): Promise<string> { const authHeader = ctx.request.headers.get("Authorization"); if (!authHeader) return "anonymous"; const token = authHeader.replace("Bearer ", ""); const payload = JSON.parse(atob(token.split("."))); return payload.groups?. ?? "unknown"; } }With this function deployed, an administrator can create an HTTP policy rule: Custom Function "JWT Role" contains "finance_contractor" with an action of Allow. The custom function becomes part of the rule condition, evaluated alongside every other selector.Custom functions are not limited to HTTP traffic. Because they receive identity, device posture, and connection metadata instead of the full HTTP request, you can use them in the Gateway Network policy rule builder with arbitrary Layer 4 port and protocol traffic as well.The Worker itself can do anything a Worker can already do — call external APIs, read from KV or D1, or invoke Workers AI. But from Gateway's perspective, the function is deterministic: data in, value out.When to use a custom function or a Forward actionCustom functions are designed for quick, bounded, stateless evaluations of data which can return a shaped response. You should think of their use similarly to data that can already be evaluated in Gateway selectors; that is, calculations on data that exist within a set of criteria, e.g. “Ports within this range,” or “URL paths that match this regex pattern.” The power comes from being able to extend your structured evaluations with arbitrary or internal sources of data, for which you’ll see some examples below.The Forward action requires a little more planning and preparation. It can be used for powerful transformations inline with users’ live requests, and can manipulate them in complex ways both on the egress and return to the origin service. These should be thought of as transformation functions, something that very few enterprise security proxies even conceptualize today. Workers that use the Forward action should be targeted and designed carefully to avoid adverse effects on the end user’s overall experience.What you can buildPurpose justification and interstitial pagesA Worker intercepts a request to a sensitive destination and returns an interstitial page requiring the end user to provide a written justification for access. The Worker calls Cloudflare KV to write a session with a TTL, so the user is only prompted once per configured period. It writes the user's identity and their stated justification to Cloudflare D1, creating an audit trail. Or, you can use Hyperdrive to write that record to any internal database you already operate.This has been one of our most-requested features for over four years. With a Worker able to process and manipulate HTTP traffic, it's easy to build to your own standards.Dynamic HTTP header injectionA custom function parses a JWT from the request's Authorization header, extracts the user's role or group membership, and returns it as a selector value. A Gateway rule matches on that value and sets an X-App-Role header on the upstream request. No NGINX proxy pool. No additional infrastructure to maintain.File inspection and loggingWhen a file download matches certain criteria, a Worker can send the file to a third-party sandboxing service for detonation and analysis. Or it can write the file in its entirety to Cloudflare R2 as a permanent record for later inspection, without the file ever leaving the Cloudflare network.Real-time alerting on policy matchA Worker bound to a Forward policy receives traffic whenever a data loss prevention (DLP) profile matches. The Worker sends a message to a Slack channel or PagerDuty endpoint with the user's email, the rule that fired, and the destination URL.export default { async invoke(ctx: GatewayContext, env: Env): Promise<void> { await fetch(env.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL, { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify({ text: `DLP alert: ${ctx.identity.email} triggered "${ctx.rule.name}" accessing ${ctx.request.url}` }) }); } }Complex evaluation logicTraditional expression builders for firewalls are not designed for the kind of computation some organizations need at evaluation time. If you maintain internal risk scoring systems that perform behavioral analysis across multiple data sources, or if you have complex maps of users, groups, and conditional memberships where multiple criteria must be independently true, you can use a custom function as the computational extension that evaluates all of that logic and returns a single value to Gateway.Performance and reliabilityBecause Gateway and Workers services run on the same machines in the Cloudflare network, dispatching to a Worker does not introduce a network hop. The performance impact is limited to the execution time of your Worker code itself.When a custom function fails — throws an exception, times out, or returns an unexpected value — you configure the fallback behavior per function. Default values are required in the custom function contract, so that it’s easy to determine behavior.Availability and pricingThe Forward action and its integration with Workers are available in a public beta starting today, with Custom Functions expected to be available before the end of the year. At general availability, both will be available for all customers on all plan types.Traffic dispatched to your Workers is billed as standard Worker requests. The feature works with Workers Free, Workers Paid, and Workers for Enterprise with no restrictions on functionality. Workers Free does have execution time limits and daily request limits, which is worth considering as you scale the volume of Gateway traffic you send to your Workers.DLP custom functions for inline detection validationA fully programmable SASE platform extends beyond just Gateway. Our DLP offering — already integrated across Gateway, AI Gateway, Email Security, and more — now supports custom outcomes through integrations with our Compute platform, as well.Most data security products operate by looking for data that matches known patterns. Customers can typically define regular expressions, word lists, or similar to operate these detections. They can also improve confidence in matching through the use of keywords or context analysis on the request body. But these methods have a core flaw: these types of detections can only tell you when something matches the pattern of data relevant to your organization, not whether this specific instance of data is indicative of data exfiltration or misuse.As attackers become increasingly advanced, and agents can be used to ruthlessly exploit systems, improving our ability to accurately detect patterns is not enough. To improve accuracy for the data that matters, you need to know whether the data in question is actively relevant to your organization.To solve this problem, most solutions leverage exact data match, but this comes with its own trade-offs. Customers must prepare, maintain, and transfer reference datasets, then decide how comfortable they are allowing a vendor to manage data from their most sensitive systems. Custom validation functions for DLP bridges that gap, and they’re available starting today. These custom functions allow customers to define their own validation logic, using their own source of truth, directly inside a Cloudflare Worker… and apply it everywhere they use DLP to protect their sensitive data.Credential and secret verificationWhen a DLP detection entry is matched, an outbound Worker can be dispatched to run validation logic prior to a policy enforcement decision. If you have profiles to detect the use of GitHub secrets, but only care about active secrets, you can use a Worker to first look up the status of a detected key, return a response from the appropriate GitHub endpoint, and then decide whether or not the DLP profile should match the traffic.import { DlpValidation, type DlpValidationInput, type DlpValidationResult, } from "@cloudflare/zt-types"; export class DlpValidationEntrypoint extends DlpValidation { async validate({ excerpt, start, end }: DlpValidationInput): Promise<DlpValidationResult> { const bytes = Uint8Array.from(atob(excerpt), (c) => c.charCodeAt(0)); const token = new TextDecoder().decode(bytes.slice(start, end)); const res = await fetch("https://api.GitHub.com/user", { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`, "User-Agent": "dlp-GitHub-validator", Accept: "application/vnd.GitHub+json", }, }); if (res.ok) return { score: 1.0 }; // token is valid and active if (res.status === 401) return { score: "veto" }; // token is invalid, discard return { score: 0 }; } }What's nextThis is just the beginning of the fully programmable SASE platform. We are actively working on increasing the entry points from which you can dispatch custom functionality to the entire Cloudflare One suite, with Email Security coming next. That doesn’t mean we’re done building: this new architecture will make it easier for us to build first-party features into all Cloudflare One services faster, more flexibly, and with improved developer experience.It’s also getting easier every day to protect your Workers, agents, and their traffic using Cloudflare One. If you are an Enterprise customer who would like a strategy session for implementation, a preview of the coming functionality, or to be notified about the custom functions beta, please reach out to your account team.Your organizational security can now do anything a Cloudflare Worker can do. We can't wait to see what you build.Review the Gateway and Workers integration documentationSee example Worker scripts for use in GatewayTeach your agent to build with Gateway and WorkersLearn more about Custom functions for DLP

title: [Cloudflare] Deploy with Void
summary:
VoidZero's tools such as Vite, Vitest, Oxc, and Rolldown — bundled in one toolchain as Vite+ — have made frontend development faster, but building full-stack applications requires more than just a tooling stack. These applications need server routes, databases, local development environments, and a fast and easy way to deploy ideas to production.We’re excited to open-source three new products that bring server routing, typed data access, and Cloudflare deployment into a unified Vite workflow.Void Platform: A shared deployment platform for teams to host Void apps on Cloudflare.Void SDK: A composable JavaScript SDK for building full-stack apps with Vite.Void CLI: A CLI for provisioning resources and deploying Vite apps to Cloudflare.The CLI deploys apps built with the SDK to the Platform. All three products are open-sourced as a single JavaScript package and Vite plugin that you can install via npm install void. With Void, you can build your server and client together, carry types from your database to the UI, and let Void automatically provision the Cloudflare resources that your app uses.We originally set out to build a single, private platform for all users to deploy apps to. After VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we adjusted our direction to open-source the platform and allow anyone to install because we saw a growing need: companies want to encourage vibe-coded internal apps, but are concerned about security and do not want to give cloud access to every employee. Void addresses this problem.Void Platform: a cloud platform for your companyThe Void Platform is fully open source and you can fork it and adapt it to your needs by integrating your company's systems, customize deployment workflows, build features for your customers, or make it work on other deployment platforms. Use the platform as it is, contribute improvements upstream, or fork it and build only the features you need. The open source code can be used out of the box or as a starting point.As an admin of a Void Platform, you control access, set resource limits, inspect deployments and usage through the Void CLI or admin dashboard, and provide guardrails so everyone else can ship serious and vibe coded apps to the same shared platform.By installing a Void Platform, your team or customers have a shared deployment environment in your Cloudflare account on top of Workers for Platforms. Void Platform enables:Faster prototyping. Your team can quickly build prototypes, deploy them, and share working apps for feedback, without setting up a separate Cloudflare account or provisioning resources for every project. This reduces the time to ship internal apps from days/weeks to minutes.Non-technical teams building. This workflow also lets teammates who do not normally write code work with coding agents to build and share their own apps. A designer can create an interactive prototype, or an operations teammate can build an internal dashboard, then deploy it to the same platform. All with the right security measures in place.To self-host a Void platform, you need:A Cloudflare account with Workers for Platforms and R2 enabledA PostgreSQL databaseAn account with your chosen login providerA domain for your appsThen install Void as a cloud platform by running a single command:Once your platform is set up, approved users can connect to it via the Void CLI for deployment.void connect https://api.orange-company.devA user builds their app using the Void SDK, which is what powers Void Platform benefits like authentication, framework detection, resource provisioning, and more. In other words, Void Platform only works because of the accompanying SDK and CLI.Void SDK: zero-config infrastructureVoid turns a Vite app into a full-stack Cloudflare Workers app. You or your agents can write code and Void will automatically infer resource bindings and provision resources such as databases, queues, or AI bindings during deployment.To get started, add Void as a Vite plugin:import { defineConfig } from "vite"; import { voidPlugin } from "void"; import { voidReact } from "@void/react/plugin"; export default defineConfig({ plugins: , });The Void SDK ships with adapters for popular JavaScript UI frameworks such as React and Vue, provides file-based API routing, pre-rendering, caching, islands, and end-to-end type safety from the database to your UI.All of Void’s features are optional and composable. Void integrates with existing application frameworks such as Vinext, React Router, SvelteKit, Nuxt, TanStack Start, and Astro. You can use those frameworks for routing and rendering, while Void handles resource APIs using Hono, migrations, deployment, and authentication with Better Auth.Let's take a look at building a server-rendered page, with types inferred from the database query through to the client:// pages/blog.server.ts import { defineHandler, type InferProps } from 'void'; import { db } from 'void/db'; import { posts } from '@schema'; export const loader = defineHandler(async () => ({ posts: await db.select().from(posts), })); export type Props = InferProps;// pages/blog.tsx export default function Blog({ posts }: Props) { return (
    {posts.map((post) =>
  • {post.title}

); }By importing void/db, Void provides a local database to your app during development and makes void deploy provision D1 automatically for you in production. This also works for using AI through Cloudflare’s AI Gateway: just by importing void/ai, everything is set up automatically for you.// routes/api/decide.ts import { defineHandler } from 'void'; import { ai } from 'void/ai'; export const POST = defineHandler(async (c) => { const { question } = await c.req.json(); const result = await ai.run('@cf/cloudflare/clef', { model: 'clef', state: {}, questions: { decision: { type: 'noul', instructions: question }, }, }); const probability = result.answers.decision.noul; return c.json({ answer: probability >= 0.5 ? 'yes' : 'no', probability, }); });Void's React router is built for Async React, using transitions and Suspense to enable responsive navigation across screens. When you pair this router with a modern data framework such as fate and UI libraries such as Astryx, you can coordinate navigation, data fetching and mutations through React's transitions, as well as actions and optimistic updates across your entire application. Together, these pieces let you build apps that feel synchronous on fast networks, gracefully fall back on slower ones, and keep interactions responsive during expensive rendering updates.If a user does not need Void Platform’s team management features, they can use their own Cloudflare account. Void SDK also deploys to Cloudflare directly.Void CLI: one deployment commandThe Void CLI is the main interface for Void. The CLI manages the platform and deploys the app. It's built on top of the new cf CLI and works well with agents.With the Void CLI, you can ask your agent to debug failing requests, read deployment logs, analyze how your app is performing, or have them take care of the full lifecycle by deploying a finished app for you. Once your app is ready to deploy to Cloudflare, you can run:The first time you run void deploy, the CLI will prompt you to log into your Cloudflare account. Void builds your app using Vite, applies migrations, automatically provisions resources, and deploys to Cloudflare or a Void Platform. It can be used to handle the full lifecycle of your project such as building, deploying, and managing your resources and projects, for example:Similar to how the CLI, and an agent by extension, can manage the entire lifecycle of a Void app, you can also use the CLI to manage a Void Platform:Manage users, project access, and resourcesInspect deployments, logs, and rollbacksMonitor platform health and usageConnect with usVoidZero’s mission is to make JavaScript developers more productive than ever before. We brought Vite, Rolldown, Oxlint, Oxfmt, and Vitest together in Vite+ for development, bundling, code quality, and testing. Void extends that stack to full-stack application development, letting you and your agents build, test, and deploy entire applications.We’ve been using the Void SDK, CLI, and Platform in production at VoidZero for the past several months and we are excited to see what you'll build with Void.
